prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength opened the 10^-18 regime of frequency metrology

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as a single-part prize and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. In answer to the chair's first question, what the citation recognises that the 2005 and 2012 prizes did not is a new kind of clock: many neutral atoms held in an optical lattice at a magic wavelength, where the light shift of the clock transition cancels, so that the statistical power of an ensemble is combined with the freedom from motional and trapping shifts that previously belonged to single trapped ions. The comb prize honoured the means of counting optical cycles and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems; neither covers this ensemble architecture or the accuracy it reached. The round-1 exchange has strengthened rather than weakened the case: the science is accepted by every member who addressed it, the disagreement is about novelty and credit, and five members now name the same two laureates with the same core credit, Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for taking the strontium lattice clock to the accuracy and stability frontier. Independent reproduction in several national laboratories removes the maturity question, and the demonstrated 10^-18 performance, with its uses in relativistic geodesy and in tests of varying constants, does not depend on the redefinition of the second. I would not make the prize wait for that administrative decision.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is still the cumulative-recognition one: a sceptic can read lattice clocks as an excellent refinement of a line already honoured in 2005 and 2012. I think that is answered by careful wording, but not entirely, and the committee should not pretend the overlap is absent. The second is credit. A two-name allocation leaves out Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Derevianko, and the weight that the lattice proposal carries against the long JILA programme is a judgement, not a fact I can read from the supplied text. Danielsson's low ranking and Eriksson's and Mehlig's preference for B038 show that this is not a unanimous case, and the fact that five of eight members converged on it should not be counted as scientific evidence in itself, since several of us come from atomic and optical physics.

responses.point: Kroll treats his support and mine as one view held twice because we share a field, and says the overlap with the 2012 prize is stronger for the trapped-ion programme than for the clocks. He also raises a possible perceived link to Jun Ye through a research stay in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I accept the point that our agreement on B002 should not be double-counted, and for that reason I have tried to test my own preference against members who are not atomic physicists, in particular Olsson and Pearce, who reached it from the maturity and reproduction arguments rather than from the atomic physics. I also agree that the novelty margin is thinner for B033 than for the clocks, and that is why I do not propose it as a second part. On his disclosure, I read a past stay in Hall's laboratory as a perceived link to be recorded and not as a reason to abstain, since he does not collaborate with Ye and his own work does not overlap with clocks. I would leave it to the chair, but I would not want the committee to lose his judgement on the credit question.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene for its conceptual economy, a minimal model organising a large phenomenology, and for the highest Borda total, while conceding that the field is about eight years old and that the pairing mechanism and Cao's role are unsettled. He says that for maturity B002 is the safer choice.
responses.response: I find the conceptual-economy argument persuasive: the Bistritzer-MacDonald model is exactly the kind of compact result that earns a prize. The chair asked what would raise B038 above B002, and my honest answer is a settled central lesson, either the pairing mechanism or a broader consensus on which correlated phases are generic. Without that the citation can only claim a platform and a prediction-plus-discovery sequence, which is real but is a statement about promise as much as about understanding. I also take the point that a high Borda total reflects breadth of second-choice support, which is not the same as being first for the same reasons. Mehlig's own concession that clocks are the safer choice on maturity is the part of his statement I weigh most. I would still keep B038 as my first alternative and would revisit it in a later year if the mechanism question closes.

responses.point: Olsson moved to B002 because it was ranked highly by members from different specialities, meets the discovery-or-invention test, and has a two-person credit that avoids the truncation problems of B017, B056, B015 and B053. She notes that Lemonde, Ludlow and Takamoto are omitted.
responses.response: I agree with her comparison of credit across the shortlist: a two-name allocation that matches the concept and the realisation is rare, and it is a legitimate scientific criterion, not just a convenience. Where I would be more cautious than her statement is on how far the omitted names are a cost. Takamoto's early strontium lattice demonstration sits close to Katori's, so the citation should be worded around the invention and realisation of the lattice clock and not around a first measurement, so that it does not make a priority claim the record cannot bear. I also note that her own first choice, B055, is one she will not advocate and would recuse on, which I think is the right handling and leaves her B002 judgement independent of it.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps the experimental Higgs discovery first on the weight of the question it answered and proposes to meet the attribution problem by tying the citation to the conception and leadership of the experiments. He lists B002 and B038 as the better-attributed alternatives.
responses.response: I accept that the weight of the Higgs discovery is greater than that of any metrological advance, and I do not dispute that scientific ranking. My difficulty is that wording the citation around conception and leadership turns the prize into a recognition of leadership roles, and the committee would then have to defend why Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, and not the discovery-year spokespersons or the analysis leaders, carry that role. His own statement that no honest three-name allocation may exist is the point I would press: if the committee cannot state a principled rule, the weight of the science cannot repair the credit problem. I would change my view only if a rule were put forward that did not depend on the three-person limit, and none has been offered in round 1. His inclusion of B002 as an alternative is something I note with some reassurance.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B038 for the cleanest theory-plus-experiment attribution, and said in his round-1 response that he could accept B002 as the second part of a two-part prize.
responses.response: I appreciate that he has left the door open to B002, and it deserves a direct answer. A two-part prize of B002 and B038 would solve the attribution problem in each part, but it would also bring the maturity problem of B038 into a prize that B002 can carry alone, and it would put five names across two fields into a configuration that I do not think the science requires. I also think the committee should avoid a combination chosen to reconcile preferences. On his substantive point that the flat-band prediction followed by the discovery is the cleanest story on the list, I agree about the story and differ only about timing. I would give his case more weight if the correlated phases proved to be reproducible and understood, and I would need to see that before ranking it above B002.

responses.point: Pearce, who moved from IceCube to B002, says that independent reproduction across several national laboratories is a stronger signal than a single flagship facility, and that the redefinition of the second is not decisive for timing.
responses.response: I am glad that he moved on this basis, since it is the argument I value most as well. I also agree with his reading of the timing question: the demonstrated performance and its independent verification are what the prize should rest on, and awaiting a metrological decision that the committee does not control would make the prize depend on something outside the science. I would add that IceCube remains a case I take seriously, and I would not want his move to hide the fact that he listed it as an alternative; his own proximity to astroparticle work is properly disclosed. I would not support it now, because the source populations behind the diffuse flux are unresolved, but I would revisit it if the 2013 detection alone were thought sufficient.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes to be a new achievement and not a continuation of the same line.

Whether the credit boundary between the lattice concept (Katori), the strontium accuracy programme (Ye) and the early contributions of Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow and Derevianko is drawn fairly; I cannot resolve priority details from the supplied text.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would strengthen or weaken the case; I judge that it is not needed but cannot prove it.
Whether the maturity of B038 will in the near future include a settled account of the correlated phases.
statement.conflict_note: My disclosure is unchanged. My profile documents training in Ingvar Lindgren's group, a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, papers with the Lund attosecond group, collaborations with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and work with Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato. None of these people is credited for B002, B038 or B033, and the profile documents no specific link to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Cirac, Zoller or Blatt. I am a theorist in atomic structure and not a clock or ion-trap collaborator, but my field is close to atomic precision physics, which the committee should keep in mind when counting the atomic-physics support for B002. I have noted Kroll's perceived link and Johansson's and Olsson's recusal statements and have no objection to them.
